Oliver — thanks for the clear ask. We're preparing a concise packet that covers: the customer‑pinned zone concept, enforcement points (VPC routing, security groups, and hypervisor-level tenant fencing), the control plane isolation model (control plane traffic to our management VPC over mutual TLS + KMS boundaries), and the emergency isolation runbook.

What I'm sending now: a first draft PDF (attached) and a short CSV with the egress allowlist. The Drive folder below contains editable diagrams if you want us to iterate: https://drive.redwood.internal/shared/1A2b_customer_pinned_zones

Attachments in this message: 20270402_customer-pinned-zones_diagram.pdf (diagram, 2 pages), egress-allowlist-matrix.csv (3 columns: source, destination, justification).

Quick highlights:
- Customer‑pinned zones: each Private tenant is assigned a VLAN and logical routing table at the edge pod. Routes to other tenants are absent by default; any cross‑tenant peering requires an explicit policy object in our central orchestration and two‑party approval.
- Control plane: our management/control plane is on a separate VPC with strict egress rules; all control messages are authenticated using client certs and signed tokens. No customer data flows into the control plane.
- KV cache and model artifacts: stored encrypted per‑tenant (KMS‑wrapped keys); backups are stored in a locked bucket with ACLs restricted to our SRE KMS role.
- Incident isolation: short playbook attached in private-deploy-dataflow-notes.txt (stepwise commands to isolate a tenant, block egress, and snapshot KV cache).

We'll incorporate any feedback and produce a CAIQ‑friendly narrative section. If Thomas wants a 30m call, we can take Monday morning.

Adding a few technical clarifications for the packet — please paste these into the CAIQ answer where relevant.

1) Tenant fencing is enforced at three layers: edge router (VLAN + route table), host hypervisor (namespace isolation + cgroups), runtime (inference runtime enforces KV cache scoping). These are independent controls so compromise of one layer still leaves other fences intact.

2) Egress policies: by default no outbound routes to public internet are attached to tenant subnets. We provide an egress gateway service that performs allowlist enforcement, TLS termination for customer‑initiated outbound, and TLS inspection for telemetry endpoints (where customers opt in). The provided CSV enumerates the default allowed domains for telemetry and update endpoints (redwood‑updates.redwood.com, registry.redwood.com).

3) Control plane data flow: management API calls are over dedicated management network links. We publish flow‑logs to an audit cluster and ship immutable records to our long‑term retention archive (SIEM ID: SIEM‑REW‑2027). Evidence link: https://sig.redwood.internal/evidence/HD-98123/packet

4) Playbook excerpt: to sever tenant network in an incident:
   - run rwctl tenant isolate --tenant-id <id> --block-egress true
   - snapshot /kvcache/<tenant> to s3://redwood‑snapshots/incident‑<id>/
   - rotate tenant KMS key and confirm re‑encryption job status

I attached a minimal CSV with an extra column "enforcement_point" for your reviewers.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Head of Reliability & Security, Redwood Inference
